{"id": "69:28/q05", "question": "What does 'my wealth' encompass?", "turns_on": "Whether the relative construction and possessive wording extend māliya to followers, or the apparent wording confines it to money.", "positions": [{"id": "69:28/q05/p1", "position": "It includes worldly property and comparable assets such as followers.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī includes property and followers. {"id": "69:28/q07", "question": "What is the final hāʾ of māliyah and why is it there?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:28/q07/p1", "position": "It is hāʾ al-sakt, a pause consonant preserving the ending or its vowel.", "reasons": "Burhān says it marks a pause after a built ending, preserves its vowel, is normally dropped in connection, and is supported by codex spellings. {"id": "69:28/q08", "question": "Is the final hāʾ of māliyah retained in connected recitation?", "turns_on": "How a pausal hāʾ is handled during liaison, and which readers transmit each treatment; Abū Ḥayyān contests a claim that retaining it is erroneous.", "positions": [{"id": "69:28/q08/p1", "position": "Most readers retain the hāʾ in connection as well as at a stop.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid names Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Abū ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿĀmir, and says all retain it at pause; his listed parallels include 6:90, 69:29, and 101:10, while two other al-Ḥāqqa forms retain it in both settings. Bayḍāwī contrasts Ḥamza with other readers. Abū Ḥayyān calls retention the majority reading for book, reckoning, wealth, power, and mā hiyah. Ibn al-Jazarī likewise says the others retain it. Abū Ḥayyān rejects al-Zuhrawī's claim that connected retention is an error because the reading is mass-transmitted."}, {"id": "69:28/q08/p2", "position": "Some readers omit the hāʾ in connection, while retaining it at a stop.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid says Ḥamza omits it in the listed forms, whereas al-Kisāʾī omits it only in lam yatasannah and iqtadih and retains it in the other forms. Jishumī and Ibn al-Jazarī name Ḥamza and Yaʿqūb for māliyah, sulṭāniyah, and al-Qāriʿah's mā hiyah; Bayḍāwī names Ḥamza for both al-Ḥāqqa endings. Ibn ʿĀshūr names Ḥamza and Khalaf for māliya and sulṭāniya. Abū Ḥayyān also names Ibn Abī Isḥāq and al-Aʿmash in connected speech and says Ḥamza omits it in selected forms. Burhān says Ḥamza omits it in three words but retains it at a stop. Qiraat-ER notes that without it māliya runs into halaka."}, {"id": "69:28/q08/p3", "position": "Ibn Muḥayṣin deletes the hāʾ and makes the yāʾ quiescent.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān distinguishes this reading from those that delete the hāʾ only in connected speech."}]}
{"id": "69:28/q09", "question": "How are the adjacent hāʾ sounds in māliyah halaka pronounced?", "turns_on": "Whether the first hāʾ keeps its pausal status with a slight stop or is treated as original in uninterrupted connection.", "positions": [{"id": "69:28/q09/p1", "position": "The two hāʾs are kept clear, often with a light pause on the first.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī says most reciters use iẓhār because the first is hāʾ al-sakt. Makkī read with iẓhār and calls it correct despite his analogy favoring assimilation. Abū Shāma says iẓhār requires a slight pause, since unpaused connection requires assimilation or vocalization; al-Sakhāwī prefers stopping and, if connecting, iẓhār because the first hāʾ is notionally paused. Ibn al-Jazarī follows al-Dānī's light pause with taḥqīq. Qiraat-ER calls the standard reading a saktah before halaka. Burhān explains pausal intent for retained hāʾs in kitābiyah and ḥisābiyah."}, {"id": "69:28/q09/p2", "position": "The final hāʾ assimilates into the initial hāʾ of halaka in continuous recitation.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī reports reciters who assimilate and permits an inferred idghām in māliyah halak by analogy with qāla rajul/rajulān and qāla rabb, when it conflicts with no explicit transmission, consensus, or principle. Makkī argues that naql at kitābiyah innī treats the hāʾ as original and so calls for assimilation here, although his practice is iẓhār. Abū Shāma says true connection requires assimilation or vocalization. Ibn al-Jazarī follows al-Dānī's assimilation with ilqāʾ because the hāʾ is treated as original. Qiraat-ER describes merging the two hāʾs."}]}

{"id": "69:28/q17", "question": "How does the lament connect with its surrounding and related verses?", "turns_on": "Which contextual relation is highlighted: solitary arrival or the sequence contrasting the blessed and the wretched.", "positions": [{"id": "69:28/q17/p1", "position": "It fits the condemned person's solitary arrival before God.", "reasons": "Rāzī compares this loneliness with 19:80, 'and he comes to Us alone.'"}, {"id": "69:28/q17/p2", "position": "It contrasts the blessed person's joy and good life with the wretched person's grief before punishment.", "reasons": "Rāzī says the blessed are described eating and drinking before the wretched person's restraints and food are described."}]}

{"id": "69:29/q05", "question": "What is the final هْ in سُلْطَٰنِيَهْ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:29/q05/p1", "position": "It is hāʾ al-sakt, a pause consonant appended to the underlying form ending in -iya.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas treats it like the ending of hisabiyah (69:26). {"id": "69:29/q06", "question": "How is the final هْ read in pause and connection?", "turns_on": "Whether the pause hāʾ remains pronounced during true connection, is omitted there, or is treated as a pause with only a brief interval; reader attributions differ across the listed forms.", "positions": [{"id": "69:29/q06/p1", "position": "Retain the hāʾ both at pause and in connected recitation.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid attributes retention in the listed forms to Ibn Kathir, Nafi, Asim, Abu Amr, and Ibn Amir; al-Kisai retains it here though omitting it in lam yatasannah and iqtadih. Al-Jishumi, Ibn al-Jazari, Abu Hayyan, and al-Baydawi describe retention by other or most readers, with pause retention agreed. Abu Hayyan rejects al-Zuhrawi's claim that connected retention is erroneous: the transmitted reading is mass-transmitted and accepted. Al-Burhan says connected retention can reflect an intended pause."}, {"id": "69:29/q06/p2", "position": "Omit the hāʾ in connected recitation but retain it when stopping.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid attributes the connected omission in the listed forms to Hamza and says all keep it at pause; al-Kisai omits only in two other forms, thus retaining it here. Al-Jishumi and Ibn al-Jazari include Yaqub with Hamza for maliyah, sultaniyah, and ma hiyah. Ibn Ashur names Hamza and Khalaf. Abu Hayyan also names Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-A'mash for connected omission and says Hamza selects particular forms. Al-Burhan reports Hamza's three-word omission while distinguishing kitabiyah and hisabiyah. Qiraat-ER likewise records omission in connection and retention at pause."}, {"id": "69:29/q06/p3", "position": "Ibn Muhaysin deletes the hāʾ and makes the yāʾ silent.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan distinguishes Ibn Muhaysin's form from the omission only in connected speech ascribed to Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-A'mash."}, {"id": "69:29/q06/p4", "position": "Stop on the hāʾ, or make an intentional light pause, when using the written pause ending.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan says true connection would require deletion by Arabic grammar whereas stopping honors grammar and codex spelling; he interprets reported connection as reciting with pausal intention and a brief interval. Al-Sakhawi prefers stopping because the hāʾ was added for pause. Ibn al-Jazari follows al-Dani in making a light pause under tahqiq while notionally connecting. This recommendation differs from a claim that transmitted connected retention is invalid, which Abu Hayyan rejects."}]}
{"id": "69:29/q07", "question": "How is the junction of مَالِيَهْ and هَلَكَ recited?", "turns_on": "Whether the first hāʾ remains a separate pause consonant, merges with the verb's hāʾ under true connection, or is deleted.", "positions": [{"id": "69:29/q07/p1", "position": "Keep the two hāʾ sounds distinct with iẓhār and a light pause.", "reasons": "Makki reports reading with izhar and calls it correct even though he argues that naql in kitabiyah would imply assimilation here. Ibn al-Jazari follows al-Dani: under tahqiq make a light pause on the first hāʾ while notionally connecting. Abu Shama says izhar needs a slight pause and otherwise becomes an unrecognized pause. Al-Alusi calls Abu Amr's reported assimilation weak because the pause hāʾ must be distinct."}, {"id": "69:29/q07/p2", "position": "Assimilate the pause hāʾ into the initial hāʾ of هَلَكَ in true connection.", "reasons": "Makki argues that naql in kitabiyah treats its hāʾ as original and would require assimilation in maliyah halaka, although he himself reads izhar. Abu Shama says true connection must assimilate or vocalize the sound; Ibn al-Jazari prefers assimilation with ilqa because the hāʾ is then treated as original. Qiraat-ER describes a geminated consonant. {"id": "69:29/q08", "question": "What effect do the hāʾ endings have in this judgment scene?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:29/q08/p1", "position": "Their sound evokes exhausted people's sighs, hardship, and pain during the long judgment ordeal.", "reasons": "Al-Samarrai links the endings in the resurrection scene, including 69:19 and 69:26, to psychological exhaustion and the long severe wait for intercession, citing also 70:4, 74:9, and 76:10 across the two notes."}]}
{"id": "69:29/q09", "question": "Whom is the speaker said to represent?", "turns_on": "Whether named occasion reports identify a specific man or the lament is read as representing a broader class; arguments about all condemned persons bear on the scope.", "positions": [{"id": "69:29/q09/p1", "position": "A report identifies him with Abu Jahl ibn Hisham.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi transmits this identification without further grounds."}, {"id": "69:29/q09/p2", "position": "The verse was revealed concerning al-Aswad ibn Abd al-Asad.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi attributes this to al-Dahhak; al-Kashshaf and al-Alusi attribute it to Ibn Abbas."}, {"id": "69:29/q09/p3", "position": "It portrays wealthy Quraysh leaders and other rulers who relied on worldly power.", "reasons": "Bursevi mentions leaders such as al-Walid, whose worldly standing is exposed; Elmalili describes rulers who oppressed others and trusted that their own wealth and rule would protect them."}, {"id": "69:29/q09/p4", "position": "It applies to the condemned generally, including people who never ruled a town.", "reasons": "Qatada argues that not every person entering Hell was a village ruler, since all had control of their bodies; Abu Hayyan says Ibn Abbas's proof reading covers all the damned, while Bursevi says the left-hand record belongs to all the wretched, and al-Alusi weighs the same issue."}]}
{"id": "69:29/q10", "question": "What is reported about ʿAḍud al-Dawla and this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:29/q10/p1", "position": "After boasting of his power and mastery of fate in verse, the ruler went mad and could utter or repeat only this lament.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf calls him Fannā Khusraw or al-ʿAḍud and says his poem boasted of power; Abu Hayyan calls him ʿAbd al-Dawla ibn Nuwayh, styled King of Kings, and says he failed and went mad. {"id": "69:29/q12", "question": "How does the neighboring expression mā shape this lament?", "turns_on": "Whether mā is taken as interrogative or negative.", "positions": [{"id": "69:29/q12/p1", "position": "As a question, it expresses yearning and longing.", "reasons": "Islahi says mā can be interrogative and prefers this reading for the emotional force it gives the speaker's lament in the preceding line."}, {"id": "69:29/q12/p2", "position": "As a negation, it denies that the preceding wealth helped.", "reasons": "Islahi acknowledges the negative construal of mā as the alternative to the question."}]}
{"id": "69:29/q13", "question": "How does the verse fit the surrounding judgment scene?", "turns_on": "The notes supply different links to the preceding wealth lament and to the paired portraits of the blessed and wretched.", "positions": [{"id": "69:29/q13/p1", "position": "The loss of wealth leads to the loss of the authority gained through it; neither remains useful.", "reasons": "Al-Biqai says wealth had been a means to power but cannot preserve that power now; supporters are farther away. {"id": "69:29/q14", "question": "How does this example of failed authority relate to the wider account of disbelief?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:29/q14/p1", "position": "Disbelief is broader than explicit denial; helpless wealth, followers, authority, gods, and intercessors show why one instance can be called denial.", "reasons": "Al-Samarrai compares 3:10 on wealth and children with 14:21, 11:101, 53:26, and 8:54 on other failed sources of help."}]}
{"id": "69:30/q01", "question": "Who receives the order to seize him?", "turns_on": "Whether the addressee is the infernal guard collective, each keeper summoning helpers, or an angel in al-Qashani's inward reading.", "positions": [{"id": "69:30/q01/p1", "position": "God addresses the keepers of Hell or angels assigned to the condemned.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Thaʿlabi, al-Wahidi, Ibn ʿAtiyya, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, al-Bursevi, al-Alusi, al-Tabatabaʾi, and Study Quran identify the infernal keepers or angels. {"id": "69:30/q02", "question": "Who is the one seized?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun is identified by the surrounding left-hand account or by reports naming Abu Jahl.", "positions": [{"id": "69:30/q02/p1", "position": "The condemned man whose record came in his left hand and whose wealth and power failed him.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevi identifies the disobedient recipient of the left-hand record; Elmalili identifies the speaker lamenting his useless wealth and power; Kur'an Yolu places the command after his account. {"id": "69:30/q03", "question": "What does taking him involve?", "turns_on": "Whether the seizure describes bodily custody or the inward condition of the soul.", "positions": [{"id": "69:30/q03/p1", "position": "Seize him physically, gripping him and taking him toward Hell.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur glosses taking as gripping by hand. {"id": "69:30/q04", "question": "What is reported to happen when the command to seize him is given?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in number, in whether they speak of angels or tormentors, and in what they do.", "positions": [{"id": "69:30/q04/p1", "position": "One hundred thousand angels rush upon him and bind his hand or hands to his neck.", "reasons": "Al-Tustari adds that one angel could grasp the earth with its mountains and seas, and says he is then cast into Hell. {"id": "69:30/q09", "question": "What sequence do fa and the repeated thumma convey?", "turns_on": "Whether thumma principally intensifies the pictured punishments or links reconstructed commands; both analyses give fa immediate force.", "positions": [{"id": "69:30/q09/p1", "position": "Shackling follows seizure immediately; the later thumma marks escalating terror, not a pause between punishments.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur says fa signals speed; Elmalili and al-Bursevi say the hands are bound without delay. {"id": "69:30/q10", "question": "How does the command contribute to the passage's cadence and order?", "turns_on": "For the following command's fronting, whether verse-ending cadence or special emphasis explains its order.", "positions": [{"id": "69:30/q10/p1", "position": "The command is an example of a balanced cadence followed by a longer third clause.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan contrasts the longer third clause here and in 69:31 with a longer second clause in 'Your companion has neither strayed nor erred.'"}, {"id": "69:30/q10/p2", "position": "The following Fire command fronts 'the Fire' to preserve aligned verse endings.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan says 'roast him in the Fire' would convey the sense but lose the joined cadence. {"id": "69:30/q12", "question": "How does this command connect to the preceding account?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize different triggers or narrative links: the books and warning, testimony of limbs, failed wealth and power, or scorn of the guards.", "positions": [{"id": "69:30/q12/p1", "position": "After the two groups are described by their books, the command warns sinners of prepared punishment.", "reasons": "Jishumi states this link to the earlier presentation of the two groups."}, {"id": "69:30/q12/p2", "position": "The man's limbs testify to his association of partners with God, prompting the order.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawi reports this from Muqatil."}, {"id": "69:30/q12/p3", "position": "The command turns on the left-hand recipient's failed wealth and power.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevi identifies him by his left-hand record; Elmalili says he has just lamented his useless wealth and power and hears the command as though they were addressed; Kur'an Yolu places it after his account."}, {"id": "69:30/q12/p4", "position": "The condemned man is handed to guards he had previously scorned.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi says he had scorned the zabaniya when they were mentioned."}]}
{"id": "69:31/q01", "question": "What does ثُمَّ signal between the punishments?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:31/q01/p1", "position": "It marks an increase in the severity or terror of successive punishments, without requiring a delay between them.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and Bursawī explicitly contrast escalation with elapsed time; Bursawī says the threatening scene allows no pause. {"id": "69:31/q02", "question": "How can ثُمَّ and the following ف connect the commands?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:31/q02/p1", "position": "Unspoken successive orders to the wardens allow ثُمَّ to link the orders while ف marks their immediate execution.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Shaykh, as reported by Bursawī, supplies the omitted commands to avoid coordinating both particles on a single clause."}]}
{"id": "69:31/q03", "question": "What is ٱلْجَحِيمَ here?", "turns_on": "Whether al-Jaḥīm denotes Hell's great fire generally or a specific level or gate; the notes supply no argument deciding its precise location.", "positions": [{"id": "69:31/q03/p1", "position": "Hell as an immense, fiercely blazing fire, described by some as its greatest or most severe fire.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī calls it a name for Hell and a great fire, near in sense to al-saʿīr and al-waqūd. {"id": "69:31/q13", "question": "How does the clause fit the passage's cadence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:31/q13/p1", "position": "The command illustrates a cadence in which balanced wording is followed by a longer third clause.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān contrasts a longer second clause, exemplified by mā ḍalla ṣāḥibukum wa-mā ghawā, with the longer third clause in the commands to take and bind the condemned man; the note mentions 69:30–31."}]}

{"id": "70:10/q01", "question": "How is yasʾalu and the clause read?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb has fatḥa or ḍamma on yāʾ, and whether the second ḥamīm is included; al-Farrāʾ disputes the passive's compatibility with the received explanation and readers' agreement.", "positions": [{"id": "70:10/q01/p1", "position": "The verb is active: a close person does not ask another.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ says the readers agree on the active form and rejects the passive as contrary to the explanation; Ibn ʿAṭiyya names the seven readers, al-Ḥasan, Medinans, Ṭalḥa and others; Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Jishumī and al-Biqāʿī call it the majority or general reading. The active wording is explained as failure to ask after another or seek help, owing to personal preoccupation."}, {"id": "70:10/q01/p2", "position": "The verb is passive: a close person is not asked about another, summoned, or made answerable for another.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr through al-Bazzī is named by al-Wāḥidī and al-Baghawī; al-Jishumī adds al-Barjamī from ʿĀṣim and al-Ḥasan. Al-Farrāʾ objects that it conflicts with the exegesis and readers' agreement."}, {"id": "70:10/q01/p3", "position": "A reported reading omits the second ḥamīm.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says the shorter wording yields the sense that intimates recognize one another, consonant with 'they see them' in 70:11; he contrasts a reading retaining the second ḥamīm, whose syntax yields the sense that a relative does not ask about a relative."}, {"id": "70:10/q01/p4", "position": "A reported reading retains the second ḥamīm.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj contrasts it with the reading that omits the word and says its construction means no relative asks about a relative; he suggests angels are those being seen in 70:11."}]}
{"id": "70:10/q02", "question": "How does saʾala govern ḥamīman and any unspoken complement?", "turns_on": "Whether ḥamīman is the person directly asked or an 'about' complement after deletion of a preposition, and how that deletion works with the passive.", "positions": [{"id": "70:10/q02/p1", "position": "Ḥamīman is the direct object: one asks a close person, with the thing asked left understood.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī illustrates asking Zayd about his state or affairs.
